prompt: MEND
explanation: To mend a fence or a torn sleeve is to put it back in working order, which is what "repair" names. "Polish" improves the surface of something already whole, "gather" brings things together, and "borrow" takes a thing only for a time; none of the three restores what was broken.

prompt: HAVEN
explanation: A haven is a place one goes to be safe, and "refuge" names exactly that shelter from danger. "Burden" is a weight carried, "rumor" an unverified report, and "voyage" a journey — a person may have all three and still have nowhere safe to go.

prompt: MEAGER
explanation: A meager portion or a meager income is far less than what is needed, which is the sense of "scanty." "Hasty" describes the speed with which a thing is done, "murky" how clear it is, and "stale" how fresh; a meal can be any of those and still be generous in amount.

prompt: PLACID
explanation: A placid lake or a placid temperament is undisturbed, and "calm" carries that exactly. "Vacant" means empty rather than untroubled, "glossy" describes a shining surface, and "remote" describes distance; a lake can be all three and still be whipped into waves.

prompt: SQUANDER
explanation: To squander an inheritance is to spend it on nothing worth having, which is what "waste" says. "Hoard" runs the other way, keeping rather than spending; "inherit" is how one may come by the money in the first place; and "conceal" says only that no one else knows about it.

prompt: CURTAIL
explanation: To curtail a program is to cut it back before it has run its full course, and "shorten" names that reduction. "Delay" moves a program later without making it any smaller, and "approve" and "announce" are things done to a program that leave its length untouched.

prompt: TENUOUS
explanation: A tenuous connection is so slight that it barely holds, which is what "flimsy" says of a thread or an argument. "Tangled" describes a connection that is complicated rather than weak, "sullen" a mood, and "gaudy" a showy appearance — a thread can be gaudy and still hold.

prompt: EXACERBATE
explanation: To exacerbate an injury or a dispute is to make an already bad thing worse, which is the sense of "aggravate." "Postpone" puts the trouble off, "obscure" hides it from view, and "anticipate" only expects it; none of the three adds to the harm.

prompt: NOVICE
explanation: A novice is someone new to an activity and still learning it, which "beginner" names directly. A "rival" competes at it, a "spectator" watches it, and a "sponsor" pays for it — and each of the three may have followed the activity for decades.

prompt: CANDOR
explanation: Candor is the habit of saying plainly what one thinks, even when it is unwelcome, which is what "frankness" names. "Courtesy," "patience," and "modesty" are admired qualities too, but each of them is as easily shown by a person who says nothing at all.

prompt: RESOLUTE
explanation: A resolute person holds to a decision and is not moved off it, which is what "steadfast" says. "Courteous" describes manners, "inquisitive" a taste for asking questions, and "sociable" a liking for company; a person can be all three and give way at the first objection.

prompt: ABSTAIN
choices: to take on more than one can manage
to set something aside for later use
to hold oneself back from something
to give a full account of something
correct_answer: to hold oneself back from something
explanation: To abstain is to choose not to take or do a thing that is there to be taken, which is what "to hold oneself back from something" describes. "To take on more than one can manage" is an excess rather than a refusal, "to set something aside for later use" is saving rather than declining, and "to give a full account of something" concerns telling, not doing.

prompt: RETICENT
choices: unable to reach a firm decision
quick to take offense at small things
eager to please those in authority
explanation: A reticent person keeps his own affairs to himself, which "unwilling to speak about oneself" states. "Unable to reach a firm decision" describes indecision, "quick to take offense at small things" describes touchiness, and "eager to please those in authority" describes deference — and a person may be talkative and still be any of the three.

prompt: PRUDENT
explanation: Prudence is weighing consequences before acting, which is what "showing care for the consequences" names. "Showing skill with one’s hands," "showing delight in another’s success," and "showing curiosity about foreign customs" are all real qualities, but a person may have all three and still act without a thought for tomorrow.

prompt: ANOMALY
choices: a thing repeated at regular intervals
a thing that departs from the usual pattern
a thing produced as a by-product of another
a thing valued far above what it cost
correct_answer: a thing that departs from the usual pattern
explanation: An anomaly is the case that does not fit what is otherwise observed, which "a thing that departs from the usual pattern" states. "A thing repeated at regular intervals" is the pattern itself rather than the exception to it, "a thing produced as a by-product of another" concerns origin, and "a thing valued far above what it cost" concerns worth.

prompt: Though the recipe in the book ran to a dozen steps, the version the cook made at home was -------, and she had the whole dish on the table before her guests had finished their first drink.
explanation: The dish reaches the table before a first drink is finished, so the home version must have cut the book’s dozen steps down, and "simpler" is the only choice that names that reduction. "Older," "richer," and "spicier" all describe versions that could take just as long to make.

prompt: Although the committee had spent eleven months gathering testimony, its final recommendation struck observers as -------, and more than one member complained that a year of work had produced two paragraphs anyone could have written in an afternoon.
explanation: Eleven months of testimony set against two paragraphs anyone could write in an afternoon points to work done far too quickly for the effort behind it, which is "cursory." "Contentious" would mean it provoked argument, "belated" that it came late, and "provisional" that it was offered only for now; none of the three says the recommendation was thin.

prompt: His colleagues wrote up the discovery in language of open wonder; Okonjo's own notebook gives the instrument reading, the date, and not one word about what either might mean, which beside their pages reads as -------.
explanation: The notebook gives a reading and a date and nothing else, which is writing stripped to the minimum: "spare." "Florid" describes the ornamented style his colleagues used, "jubilant" names the wonder he withholds, and "hedged" would mean he had qualified a claim — but a reading and a date make no claim to qualify, they are simply bare.

prompt: Because the trail crossed six streams swollen with snowmelt, the guides warned that the morning's crossings would be -------, and they told each hiker to pack a change of dry clothes near the top of the bag.
explanation: Six streams swollen with snowmelt, and an instruction to keep dry clothes within reach, describe crossings likely to put a hiker in the water, which is "treacherous." "Unavoidable" says only that the streams must be crossed, "picturesque" praises the view, and "monotonous" would make the warning pointless.

prompt: Since the museum could put on view only a twentieth of what it owned, and since what she settled on in the storerooms shaped whatever a generation of visitors took the collection to be, the curator's central task was in the end -------.
explanation: If nineteen objects in twenty must stay in storage, the work that decides what any visitor ever sees is choosing among them, which is "selection." "Restoration," "acquisition," and "attribution" are all genuine curatorial work, but none of them is the task created by owning far more objects than wall.

prompt: The pump had been running dry for three days, so by the time the mechanic reached the site the damage was -------, and the seal she had driven out to replace would have made no difference at all.
explanation: If replacing the seal would now make no difference, the harm has gone past the point where the original repair reaches it: "irreversible." "Superficial" would mean the repair still worked, "intermittent" describes damage that comes and goes, and "predictable" describes only whether anyone saw it coming.

prompt: The instructions taped to the copier were -------: nothing on any of the four cards ran longer than six words, and the cards were numbered in order.
explanation: Four numbered cards, none of them longer than six words, describe directions as simple as directions get, which is "elementary." "Illegible" would mean the words could not be made out at all, and "outdated" and "unofficial" concern the age and the authority of the cards rather than how easy they are to follow.

prompt: Her reply to the invitation was -------: she thanked us warmly for thinking of her, mentioned that the date fell in a difficult week, and left it entirely unsettled whether she meant to come.
explanation: She answers at length and still leaves the one question — will she come — unsettled, which is what "evasive" names. "Gracious" fits the thanks but not the silence at the end, "blunt" is the opposite of a reply this padded, and "belated" would describe when the reply arrived rather than what it did.

prompt: The general's memoir is ------- in a way his admirers have never quite acknowledged: every decision that turned out well is narrated in the first person, and every one that did not is charged to the weather, to London, or to the men.
explanation: Successes told in the first person and failures charged to the weather, to London, and to the men make a memoir arranged to flatter its author: "self-serving." "Long-winded" describes length, "ill-tempered" describes tone, and "second-hand" would mean he had not been there; none of the three explains the split between the two kinds of decision.

prompt: Neither survivor denies anything the other reports, but each gives most of his page to what the other passes over in a single line; the two accounts are less ------- than -------.
explanation: Neither man denies the other, so the accounts do not conflict; each covers what the other leaves out, so together they make one fuller picture — "contradictory ... complementary." "Detailed ... exhaustive" sets up no contrast at all, "hostile ... affectionate" describes feeling rather than content, and "rehearsed ... spontaneous" describes how the accounts were produced.

prompt: Because the ledger's entries had been made in ------- hand, the auditors could not ------- even the largest of the payments, and the firm's own accountants gave up after a week.
explanation: Handwriting that defeats the auditors and the firm’s own accountants alike must be hard to read, and what they fail at is following the payments through the book: "a cramped ... follow." "A practiced ... dispute" makes the writing easy and the failure one of disagreement, "an unsteady ... approve" turns the task into granting permission, and "a borrowed ... record" would mean the entries had yet to be written down at all.

prompt: The society's charter was ------- enough that two factions could each read it as ------- their own position, which is how a document meant to settle the quarrel came to supply both sides with ammunition.
explanation: A charter that arms both sides of a quarrel must be open to more than one reading, and each faction must be able to find its own view backed in it: "ambiguous ... endorsing." "Precise ... contradicting" would leave neither side supported, "brief ... postponing" describes delay rather than a reading, and "famous ... restating" says nothing about why two readings were possible.

prompt: Every drawer in the workshop carried a label, every tool hung on its own outlined hook, and the floor had been swept before the last of the sawdust settled; visitors found the old man almost -------.
explanation: Labeled drawers, outlined hooks, and a floor swept before the sawdust has landed are the marks of someone exacting about small details, which is "fastidious." "Reckless" runs the other way entirely, and "secretive" and "generous" describe what a man shares rather than how he keeps his shop.

prompt: Kwan spent eleven years translating a poet almost nobody reads, turned down every offer to cut the manuscript in half, and brought it out with a press that ran four hundred copies; whatever else the project was, it was not -------.
explanation: Eleven years, a poet nobody reads, a refusal to cut the book, and a print run of four hundred are all choices that cost more than they can return, so the one thing the project cannot be called is "opportunistic." "Controversial," "collaborative," and "experimental" are none of them ruled out by the sentence — a long and unprofitable translation could be any of the three.

prompt: The argument that seemed ------- when Halloran first put it forward in 1954 is now set out in every introductory textbook, its conclusions repeated as settled fact by students who have never heard his name.
explanation: An argument now repeated as settled fact must once have been received the other way, as an offense against what everyone then believed, which is "heretical." "Derivative" would mean it was unoriginal, which is no bar to a textbook, and "tedious" and "imprecise" describe faults a textbook argument could equally have kept.
